General health · published research

Adipose tissue inflammation

Summary of the Evidence

One 2016 publication examined adipose-tissue inflammation in male mice with diet-induced obesity and hyperglycemia. It reported abdominal-fat histology and blood glucose shortly after the final treatment. No human study was identified (Yoshimura et al. 2016).

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study has tested PBM for adipose-tissue inflammation in people. The mouse findings do not establish effects on human body fat, diabetes control, or inflammatory disease.

Animal evidence

Untreated obese mice had abdominal adipose inflammatory areas almost five times greater than those in the irradiated group (p < 0.001). Blood glucose was also lower in treated mice 24 hours after the final session (p = 0.04). The experiment did not establish that reduced inflammatory infiltration caused the glucose difference or that glycemic effects persisted (Yoshimura et al. 2016).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The experiment used an 843-nm near-infrared LED at 60 mW, 19 mW/cm², and 5.7 J/cm². Each exposure lasted 300 seconds, and the mice received six sessions during the four-week experiment. Light was delivered over the abdominal region. The study did not compare wavelengths or doses, and the mouse exposure does not establish how much light would reach human adipose tissue at different depths (Yoshimura et al. 2016).

Interpretation

The treated mice had less abdominal-fat inflammatory infiltration and lower glucose at one short-term measurement. These favorable findings come from one animal experiment and do not establish a durable metabolic effect or a benefit in people.

Publications and records

1 publication

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for reduced adipose inflammation and short-term glucose levels in obese mice

The finding comes from one short mouse experiment (Yoshimura et al. 2016).

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One mouse experiment found markedly smaller inflammatory areas in abdominal fat and lower blood glucose 24 hours after the final session. Confidence is very low because the finding has not been independently replicated, follow-up was short, and no human study has tested adipose or metabolic outcomes (Yoshimura et al. 2016).
